beats.lead: You have almost exactly as many bacterial cells as human ones, not ten times as many.
beats.text: A rigorous 2016 recalculation put the ratio at close to 1:1, overturning a figure that had been repeated in textbooks for decades.
beats.note: The old 10:1 figure traces back to a rough 1972 estimate that was never meant as a precise count.

beats.context: roughly how many bacterial cells researchers now estimate live in and on a reference adult body, against about 30 trillion human cells of its own.

beats.name: Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo
beats.role: recalculated both cell populations from scratch for a modelled 70kg adult and published the revised, far closer ratio in the journal PLOS Biology.

beats.text: Most of that human cell count is not skin, muscle or brain. Roughly 90 percent of it is blood, specifically red blood cells made by the bone marrow.
beats.note: The haematopoietic, or blood-forming, lineage dominates the human side of the count almost entirely.

beats.text: The exact ratio still shifts from person to person depending on body size and gut microbiome, so 1:1 is a far better rule of thumb than 10:1, not a fixed law.

beats.line: You are roughly as much bacteria as you are you.
